lead: This unit shows how to find member forces in pin-jointed trusses, analyse frames and machines, and solve dry-friction problems. After it you can take a truss apart by joints or sections, separate a frame into members, and handle inclined planes, wedges, ladders, belts and screw jacks with friction.
about: Chapter 3.1 starts with simple trusses and the method of joints. 3.2 adds the method of sections for cutting a few members. 3.3 moves to frames and machines, where members are not all two-force. 3.4 states the laws of dry friction and defines coefficient and angle of friction. 3.5 applies them to a block on a rough incline, including the range of force for equilibrium. 3.6 and 3.7 extend the same free-body method to wedges and ladders. 3.8 treats belt friction for flat and V-belts. 3.9 closes with the screw jack, using the same friction angle to find torque, effort, efficiency and self-locking.

chapters.idea: A simple pin-jointed truss is solved joint by joint using two equilibrium equations per joint.
chapters.depth: Cover the assumptions of a simple truss: light straight members, pin joints, loads only at joints. Define a perfect truss by m = 2j − 3, where m is the number of members and j is the number of joints. Use tension positive and compression negative. Find support reactions first, then draw a free-body diagram of each joint. Include zero-force members. Some syllabi call this the method of joints.

figure.aria: A triangular pin-jointed truss with joints A, B, C, a 10 kN downward load at C, and supports at A and B.

chapters.example: A pin-jointed truss has joints A(0,0), B(4,0), C(2,3); members AC, BC, AB; a 10 kN load acts vertically down at C; A is a pin and B is a roller on the horizontal. Find the forces in AC, BC and AB by the method of joints. Answers: AC = BC = −6.01 kN (compression), AB = +3.33 kN (tension).
chapters.trap: Forgetting the support reactions before starting at a joint, or treating a compression member as tension without keeping the sign.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: equilibrium of a particle. Unit 2: free-body diagrams and support reactions.
chapters.leave: Method of sections and frames to 3.2 and 3.3; friction to 3.4 onward.

chapters.idea: A section cuts a truss into two free bodies and uses three equilibrium equations to find a few member forces directly.
chapters.depth: Teach when to use a section instead of joints: when only a few member forces are wanted. A section should cut at most three unknown members. Draw the free body of one part, include external reactions and loads on that part, then use ΣM about a clever point, ΣFx and ΣFy. Some syllabi call this the method of sections. Include a check by joint equilibrium.

figure.aria: A two-panel truss with dashed cut members EF, CE and BC, a 10 kN downward load at E, and a roller at C.

chapters.example: In the truss A(0,0), B(2,0), C(4,0), D(0,3), E(2,3), F(4,3) with members AB, BC, DE, EF, AD, BE, CF, AE, CE, a 10 kN load acts downward at E; A is a pin and C is a roller. Find the force in member CE by a vertical section cutting EF, CE and BC. Answer: CE = −6.01 kN (compression).
chapters.trap: Cutting more than three unknown members, or omitting a support reaction from the chosen free body.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 method of joints; Unit 2 equilibrium of rigid bodies.
chapters.leave: Frames and machines to 3.3; friction to 3.4 onward.

chapters.idea: A frame or machine must be separated into members because not every member is a two-force member.
chapters.depth: Distinguish a truss from a frame: a frame has at least one member with forces at three or more points or a load along its length. A machine is a frame with moving parts, analysed in equilibrium. Identify two-force members first. Draw a free-body diagram of each member, show pin forces as equal and opposite, and solve the equilibrium equations. Some syllabi call this frames and machines.

figure.aria: A horizontal beam AB pinned at A and joined by a two-force link BC to a pin at C, with a 12 kN downward load at B.

chapters.example: A frame has horizontal member AB of length 3 m pinned at A. A two-force link BC of length 5 m connects B to a pin C at (0,4) m. A 12 kN load acts vertically down at B. Find the reaction at A and the force in link BC. Answers: link BC = 15 kN tension; reaction at A = 9 kN horizontal.
chapters.trap: Treating a member with a load along its length or with three pins as a two-force member.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: equilibrium of rigid bodies, free-body diagrams, two-force and three-force bodies.
chapters.leave: Friction and machines with friction to 3.4 onward; dynamics of machines to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Dry friction opposes impending motion and is limited by μN, with angle of friction φ = tan⁻¹ μ.
chapters.depth: Define static, kinetic and limiting friction. State the laws of Coulomb friction: friction acts opposite impending motion; limiting friction is proportional to normal reaction; it is nearly independent of contact area. Define coefficient μ = F/N and angle of friction φ = tan⁻¹ μ. Define angle of repose α = tan⁻¹ μ for a block on an incline. Explain that static friction is larger than kinetic friction. Some syllabi call this Coulomb friction.

figure.aria: A graph of friction force against applied force: static friction rises with applied force to 80 N, then kinetic friction drops to 60 N.

chapters.example: A 200 N block rests on a horizontal floor with μs = 0.4 and μk = 0.3. Find the limiting friction, the friction when the applied horizontal force is 60 N, and the angle of friction. Answers: limiting friction = 80 N; friction at 60 N = 60 N; φ = 21.8°.
chapters.trap: Using μk while the block is still static, or using N = W when the surface is inclined.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: equilibrium of a particle. Unit 2: free-body diagrams.
chapters.leave: Inclined plane, wedge, ladder, belt and screw jack to 3.5 to 3.9.

chapters.idea: On a rough incline the normal reaction is W cos θ, so the friction limit is μW cos θ and the safe range of applied force is fixed.
chapters.depth: Resolve the weight W into W sin θ along the plane and W cos θ normal to it. Use N = W cos θ. For impending motion down the plane, friction acts up the plane; for impending motion up, friction acts down. Derive the range P_min = W sin θ − μW cos θ to P_max = W sin θ + μW cos θ for a force P parallel to the plane. Include the angle of repose. Some syllabi call this equilibrium on a rough inclined plane.

figure.title: Block on a rough incline
figure.aria: A block on a rough incline with weight 100 N, angle 30 degrees, normal 86.6 N, friction limit 26.0 N, and the force range 24.0 N to 76.0 N.

chapters.example: A 100 N block lies on a plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. μs = 0.3. Find the range of a force P applied parallel to the plane that keeps the block in equilibrium. Answer: 24.0 N ≤ P ≤ 76.0 N.
chapters.trap: Using N = W instead of W cos θ, or putting friction in the wrong direction for impending motion.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.4 laws of friction; Unit 2 equilibrium of a particle.
chapters.leave: Wedge and ladder to 3.6 and 3.7; belt and screw to 3.8 and 3.9.

chapters.idea: A wedge uses two rough faces to turn a small pushing force into a large normal force.
chapters.depth: Draw separate free-body diagrams of the wedge and the block. Show friction on both the inclined face and the horizontal face. Use the friction angle φ to combine normal and friction into one resultant on each face. Solve by force triangle or equilibrium equations for the force P to raise or lower the load. Mention self-locking of a wedge. Some syllabi call this wedge friction.

figure.title: Wedge free bodies
figure.aria: A wedge of angle 15 degrees under a 500 N block, with friction on both faces and a free-body diagram leading to the push P.

chapters.example: A wedge of angle 15° is driven under a 500 N block. The coefficient of friction on both faces is 0.25. Find the horizontal force P needed to raise the block.
chapters.trap: Putting friction on only one face, or forgetting that the normal on the inclined face is not equal to the block weight.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.4 friction laws and chapter 3.5 inclined-plane equilibrium.
chapters.leave: Ladder, belt and screw jack to 3.7 to 3.9.

chapters.idea: A ladder is a rigid body in equilibrium with friction at the floor and possibly at the wall.
chapters.depth: Draw the ladder as a rigid body. Put the floor normal and floor friction at the foot, and the wall normal at the top. If the wall is smooth, wall friction is zero. Use ΣFx, ΣFy and ΣM, usually about the floor point. Solve for the required friction and compare it with μN. Find the minimum angle or minimum μ for no slip. Some syllabi call this ladder friction.

figure.aria: A ladder leaning at 60 degrees from a rough floor at A to a smooth wall at B, with a 600 N person at P.

chapters.example: A ladder of length 5 m and weight 200 N leans against a smooth vertical wall at 60° to the horizontal. A person of weight 600 N stands 3 m along the ladder from the floor. μ at the floor is 0.3. Find whether the ladder slips. Answer: required floor friction = 265.6 N; maximum = 240 N; the ladder slips.
chapters.trap: Adding friction at a smooth wall, or measuring the person’s position along the horizontal instead of along the ladder.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.4 friction laws; Unit 2 equilibrium of rigid bodies.
chapters.leave: Belt and screw jack to 3.8 and 3.9.

chapters.idea: Belt friction over a curved contact gives an exponential tension ratio, and a V-belt increases it through the groove angle.
chapters.depth: Derive the tension ratio from a small element of belt. Use T_tight/T_slack = e^{μθ} for a flat belt, where θ is the angle of contact in radians. For a V-belt with half groove angle β, use T_tight/T_slack = e^{μθ/sin β}. Explain that the V-belt has a larger ratio for the same μ and θ. Some syllabi call this rope friction or capstan friction.

figure.aria: A plot of tight-to-slack tension ratio against contact angle for a flat belt and a V-belt with half angle 20 degrees.

chapters.example: A flat belt on a pulley has μ = 0.3, angle of contact 120°, and tight tension 500 N. Find the slack tension. Repeat for a V-belt in a 40° groove, taking half angle β = 20°. Answers: flat belt slack tension = 267 N; V-belt slack tension = 79.6 N.
chapters.trap: Putting the contact angle in degrees, or using the full groove angle instead of the half angle in the V-belt formula.
chapters.leave: Screw jack to 3.9; belt drives and power transmission to design courses.

chapters.idea: A screw jack is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder, so friction angle fixes torque, effort, efficiency and self-locking.
chapters.depth: Define lead L, mean radius r, lead angle α with tan α = L/(2πr), friction angle φ, torque T, effort P at handle radius R, mechanical advantage and efficiency. Ignore collar friction. Use T = W r tan(α + φ) to raise load W, P = T/R, efficiency η = tan α / tan(α + φ). State self-locking: φ ≥ α. Some syllabi call this a simple screw jack.

figure.title: Screw jack
figure.aria: A screw jack calculation flow with lead 5 mm, mean radius 25 mm, lead angle 1.82 degrees, friction angle 8.53 degrees, torque 45.7 N m, effort 152 N, and self-locking.

chapters.example: A screw jack has mean radius r = 25 mm and lead L = 5 mm. The coefficient of friction is 0.15. A load W = 10 kN is to be raised. Find the torque on the screw and the effort at a handle of radius R = 300 mm; state if it is self-locking. Answers: T = 45.7 N·m; P = 152 N; φ = 8.53° > α = 1.82°, so it is self-locking.
chapters.trap: Using pitch instead of lead, using diameter instead of radius, or forgetting the handle radius when finding the effort.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.4 friction laws; basic equilibrium and moments from Unit 2.
chapters.leave: Collar friction and V-thread refinements to machine-design courses.

links: Joint method gives all member forces; sections cut the same truss to get a few quickly
Truss joints are all pins; frames need members separated because some carry loads
Section free bodies become full frame member free bodies
Coefficient and angle of friction set the friction limit used on the incline
The same friction law applies on both faces of a wedge
Incline equilibrium is the base for each wedge face
Ladder uses the same limiting friction at floor and wall
Belt friction uses the same μ but over a curved contact angle
Screw jack uses friction angle φ to find torque and self-locking
